narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 51.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tips just over 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. While the average accepted student ranks around the middle of their class, you placed in the bottom decile, signaling weaker academic performance in the later stages of your studies. This had more impact than any other piece of information.

Your LSAT score and undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction. Both were slightly above the averages of students who were accepted, and each provided a modest pull toward passing the bar. Unfortunately, these positive signals were not strong enough to overcome the effect of your third-year ranking.

Given this outcome, you should focus on strengthening the areas that most affect bar success. Consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score further, or enrolling in a post-baccalaureate program that improves your academic record and demonstrates sustained high performance. These steps would directly address the factors that led to the rejection and improve your chances in a future application cycle. (218 words)
